subject: hoverPickup
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: militarized pickup converted to hover thrusters.
Style: low-poly cyberpunk.
reasoning:
I'm planning a militarized low-poly hover pickup truck model, roughly 150 parts, static with minimal joints, built from boxes and extrudes with glow details and a few textures.

I'm laying out the chassis, cab, and bed sections along the z-axis, then designing four ducted-fan thruster pods at the wheel positions with cyan glowing fan disks and mounting arms, plus an extruded silhouette for the cab profile.

Defining hull points...

Positioning windshield plane...

Now I'm planning the military styling: armor plates with hazard stripes on doors, a roof-mounted turret with gun body, barrels, and ammo box, plus a light bar, antenna, and roll-cage. I'm also adding a rocket launcher rack on the bed, a bull bar with neon strip up front, and glowing magenta/cyan headlights.

For the finish, I'm going matte olive/gunmetal with cyberpunk cyan and magenta accents, picking out a color palette of dark steel, panel gray, magenta, cyan, and hazard yellow. I'm also planning textures: a cyan reflective window gradient, hazard stripe patterns, door/hood emblem decals with a glyph and number, a glowing fan texture for thrusters, and taillight details.

Now I'm writing custom hull paint logic that countershades the body with grime buildup near the bottom, using noise and mix functions from the SDK rather than importing a prebuilt kit, plus a glow import for emissive effects. I'm also swapping the wheels for thruster pods, starting with a lathe profile defining the duct's outer and inner radii.

Adjusting lathe points to avoid self-intersection...

Now I'm designing the fan hub with two discs for top and bottom visibility, then working out strut geometry connecting the body to the pods, making sure the pod radius and mounting rod positions keep everything proportioned without clipping into the body.

I'm checking clearances between the pods and body underside, confirming the strut length, then adding armor plating details like fender boxes and side skirts using a reusable box helper function for the panels.

Now I'm outlining the hull as an extruded shape with beveled edges and hood scoop details as small boxes layered on top, confirming static parts can omit joints entirely.

Continuing on, I'm working out the front assembly—grille with glowing cyan slots, headlight boxes with white-cyan glow, and a dark bull bar bumper with magenta neon strips, tow hooks, and cone-shaped ram teeth jutting forward.

Now I'm building the cab itself: a painted extruded body, a dark roof plate, roof rack rails, and a light bar up front alternating magenta and cyan glow segments. I'm adding thin antenna rods with glowing tips and sketching out a small radar dome on the rear roof, then starting on the armored side door plating.

Working through the door armor boxes and hazard stripe sills along the sides, I'm realizing the hazard texture would stretch into overly thin diagonal lines across such a long, narrow box, so I'm switching to a repeating pattern instead.

Now I'm positioning the side windows on the cab, adjusting the plane location and size to match the sloped roof geometry, and planning a trapezoid window graphic with a dark gradient and cyan glare lines using a simple rect with a slanted front edge.

I'll simplify to a symmetric trapezoid shape for the window so both sides work with the same mirrored geometry, skip the pillar divider for now, and add the windshield glass plane slightly offset above the cab slope plus small side mirror details.

Now I'm laying out the truck bed: a floor spanning the hull top, side walls and tailgate as boxes, a headache rack with vertical posts and a top bar behind the cab, darker bed interior coloring with an accent strip on the top rail, and a rod-based roll hoop arch over the bed before moving on to a turret mount.

Then I'm designing the turret itself: a pedestal and swivel box, twin rod-based gun barrels with muzzle brakes, a side ammo drum, a hazard-striped shield plate up front, and a glowing red sensor eye, followed by a missile pod box positioned at the rear of the bed.

Now I'm working out the angled missile launcher: positioning it tilted up about 20 degrees, then building a 2x3 grid of short cylindrical tubes with glowing red inner discs and cone-shaped red missile tips, computing each tube's position using direction vectors and cross products for the local right/up axes rather than simple axis-aligned placement.

Adding rear thrusters and nozzles, then underglow neon strips along the hull sides and magenta-glowing taillight boxes at the rear.

Sizing the hood emblem to 1.2x1.2 with a stylized skull/hex-kanji design, orienting its up-vector toward the front so it reads correctly from a viewer's perspective. Then I'm moving to cyber-styled hull details like hex mesh panels and the front camera eye, plus door armor plates positioned as boxes along the hull sides.

Now I'm working out the door decal plane placement and checking that the "07" emblem with kanji texture reads correctly regardless of which side (s=±1) it's mirrored to, confirming the plane-facing geometry makes the text legible from either direction. I'm also starting to list out the texture assets needed, like window, hazard, and emblem textures.

I'm planning additional textures: a door tag with SVG lettering, a glowing fan blade circle, a grille, a tail strip, a screen, and warning decals for the tailgate. For the hull paint function, I'm mixing a dark blue-grey base with noise, darkening the bottom for grime, lightening areas facing upward, and adding subtle darker panel lines along a grid spaced every 0.9 units.

Now I'm considering a digital camo pattern for the cab using a patches-based texture function that blends several dark green and grey tones with a small gap to keep base lines minimal, then thinking about wrapping it in a cel-shaded countershade effect.

I'll make a custom paint function that layers grime on lower surfaces, top paint on upward-facing normals, and camo everywhere else, confirming the right SDK exports (mix, noise, paint, patches) are all available from the single builder module. For the antenna, I'm checking the rod helper's argument order, confirming radius is followed directly by color.

Now I'm designing the thruster nozzle as a lathed bell shape pointing backward along the z-axis, working out an outline profile that flares outward smoothly without self-intersecting as it curves from the engine mount to the bell's wide rim.

I'm also setting up the pod using a vertical lathe profile, and adding a glowing cyan torus ring around the rim for an engine-glow effect, oriented along the correct axis.

I'm adding a magenta glowing accent ring on the pod housing with dark armor paint, and sketching out overall model sizing so the hull hovers slightly above ground clearance. Now I'm starting a helper function for building box geometry.

Adding more scene details...

Still drafting SVG assets...

Writing hull paint logic...

I need to check for collisions - the pods and fan are positioned safely above the hull bottom, but the barrel extending from the turret toward the cab may be intersecting with the cab's rear geometry, so I should verify those coordinates more carefully.

Since the cab collision is an issue, I'll move the gun to a roof-mounted turret instead, positioning it so the barrels clear the windshield, and add a light bar at the rear of the roof plus a bed-mounted rocket launcher. I'm working out the turret's base ring, pedestal, gun housing dimensions and where the barrels should start from.

Now I'm placing antennas on the cab roof's rear corners, a headache rack behind the cab, and the launcher further back in the bed with angled-up tubes. I'm computing the launcher's center position and direction vector so the tubes point forward and upward, then working out the perpendicular vector to space multiple tubes side by side.

Arranging the tube array in a 3x2 grid, each tube a cylinder with a missile cone tip glowing red at its end, plus a rotated box housing behind the tubes tilted to match the upward firing angle.

Now I'm putting together the default export module function, making sure to clone materials for glow effects and only apply the painted glow to parts that actually have paint applied, sharing materials by color where possible.
